heading: Consent
intro: What a person agreed an application may ask for on their behalf. With oauth2.consentRequired ON — it is ON by default, and it is the one policy in this service that is — the authorization endpoint draws a screen the first time a given username signs in to a given client_id for a given scope, and issues nothing until they answer. Allow writes one {attribute} value per scope onto that person's own entry under ou=users; Deny returns access_denied to the client and records nothing at all. A delegated permission is recorded by its WHOLE identifier — https://example.com/write and never the bare write — because two resources may both expose a permission of the same name and a consent to one must not cover the other.
notAsked: Nothing is being asked. oauth2.consentRequired is OFF, so the authorization endpoint issues whatever is requested and this page is a record of what was agreed while it was on. Turning it back on asks again for anything not listed below — OFF does not mean everybody consented, it means nobody was asked. The switch is on
notStored: Nothing can be written down. This process has no directory installed behind the consent register, so an answer given at the screen is honoured for that one request and forgotten — every sign-in draws the screen again. That is deliberate rather than a fallback to consenting silently: an agreement that cannot be remembered is one nobody gave.
globalsHeading: Global consent — nobody is asked about these
globalsNote:
Configuration, not a record. One value per (application, scope), held as {attribute} on the APPLICATION's own entry. Everybody who signs in to that application skips the prompt for that scope, and nothing is written about anybody — so removing a row here asks everybody again, including the people who would have said yes. That is the whole difference from the table below it, where removing a row asks one person. Removing a row also revokes every token of that application carrying the scope, except for people who agreed to it themselves, and this is the only door that removes one — on this service's own console, portal or debugger too, whose sessions standing on it then end at their next renewal.

It is keyed on the PAIR and not on the scope alone: consenting read here consents it for this application, and an application registered five minutes from now that spells the same word is still asked. It is an ordinary attribute on an ordinary entry, so an ldapmodify reaches it exactly as it reaches a redirect URI, and it persists wherever the directory does.
noGlobals: Nothing is globally consented. Every person is asked about every scope the first time an application requests it, which is what this service does out of the box.
grantNote: The scope is written exactly as a client puts it in a scope parameter: openid, profile, or a whole delegated permission identifier such as https://example.com/write. It must be a legal OAuth scope token (RFC 6749 section 3.3: any printable ASCII except space, double quote and backslash), because a value with a space in it is two scopes and could never match one. A scope no application here defines a permission for is accepted rather than refused — most scopes are not permissions.
recordedHeading: Recorded consent — what people actually answered
recordedNote:
One row per (person, application, scope), and that IS the answer. A person who agreed to five scopes for one application is five rows rather than one labelled 5, because a client that later asks for a sixth is asked about the sixth alone — which is what the screen shows and what these rows have to be able to express. The timestamp is when they pressed Allow.

Revoking a row asks that one person again the next time that one application requests that one scope, and it WITHDRAWS it: every access and refresh token that application holds for them carrying the scope is revoked on every node, and the instant is written onto their entry as {attribute}, so a refresh token granted before it is refused at the token endpoint even after they agree again. Withdrawing one scope revokes the whole refresh token. Removing a global consent above does the same for everybody it covered, and oauth2.refreshRequiresConsent refuses a refresh token from the authorization endpoint that no recorded consent covers.
searchPlaceholder: a person, an application or a scope
noMatch: Nothing matches “{q}”. The search is over the person, the application and the scope.
noneRecorded: Nobody has consented anything yet. That is what a service nobody has signed in to looks like — and also what one looks like where every scope anybody has asked for is under global consent above, because an override writes nothing down.
withdrawHeading: Withdraw everything one person agreed to for one application
withdrawNote: Every recorded consent between one person and one application, in one act — what the person can do themselves from /portal/consents. Every token that application holds for them under those scopes is revoked.
forgetHeading: Forget everything one person agreed to
forgetNote: Every recorded consent for one person, in one act, so that they are asked again by every application. It is a separate control rather than a loop over the Revoke buttons above because being asked again is the one thing somebody wants after testing this screen, and doing it a row at a time for a person with thirty consents is a chore rather than a control. It reaches nothing under global consent, because there is nothing on their entry to reach.
bothHalves: Both halves are ordinary attributes on ordinary directory entries. {globalAttribute} on an application under ou=applications, {attribute} on a person under ou=users as <when> <scope> <client_id> — the client_id last, because it is the one field with no rule about what it may contain and therefore has to take the remainder of the value. GET /admin/ldap/directory shows them as they are, and they persist wherever the directory does.
notGranted: and this client has NOT been granted it — in product mode, or with oauth2.delegatedPermissionsEnforced on, the request is refused anyway, consented or not
ordinaryScope: an ordinary scope — no application here defines a permission by that name
unreadable: This value is not in the shape this service writes — something put it on the entry by hand: {raw}. It is shown rather than dropped, because a value the page silently ignored would be one somebody wrote on purpose and could not find out was being ignored. It consents nothing.
